addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit published via the long-lived
`refactor-vc-x1` bookmark (merge-only while it ran; fully
merged into main and deleted 2026-08-03 under jj.md's
long-lived bookmark discipline).

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

aiTitle: Test git push with HTTPS URL in sandbox

content.text:
Thoughts, no actions.

## The ssh theory looks right, and for two independent reasons

The sandbox spec I'm running under blocks ssh push twice over, so switching to https was a good move regardless of which mechanism was actually biting:

**Network.** The egress allowlist is host-based (`github.com`, `*.github.com`, `*.githubusercontent.com`). Host-based filtering is almost always implemented as an HTTP CONNECT proxy or a TLS-SNI filter, because those are the only places a hostname appears on the wire. SSH has no SNI and doesn't honor `HTTP_PROXY`, so there's no way for that kind of filter to recognize a port-22 connection to github.com as allowed. It would fail closed.

**Credentials.** My filesystem read policy denies `/home/wink/.ssh` wholesale, with a handful of explicit exceptions: `git-commits-wink@saville.com`, its `.pub`, `git-commits-allowed-signers`, and `known_hosts`. Your *signing* key is readable; a general auth key (`id_ed25519` or similar) is not. So even with port 22 open, the transport would have no key to offer. The fact that whoever wrote this policy had to carve out the signing key by name is itself evidence that `~/.ssh` is meant to be closed to me.

## But I don't think ssh is the whole story

Two things make me want to widen the experiment rather than treat one green push as a clean bill of health.

**The bot repo probably still points at ssh.** You changed the URL on the work repo. `.claude` is a separate jj-git repo with its own remote, and if it was cloned the same way it's still `git@github.com:...`. Since `vc-x1 push` touches both scopes, a work-repo-only fix leaves the failure exactly where it was. Worth a `jj git remote list -R .claude` before anything else.

**The bot repo may not be writable at all.** My write allowlist is essentially `.` plus `/home/wink/data/prgs/rust`, `~/.config/jj`, `~/.cargo`, and tmp. It does not include `~/.claude/projects`, and the deny-within-allow list names `/home/wink/.claude/projects` explicitly. The project-root `.claude` is a symlink into exactly that directory, and Linux sandboxing (landlock, bubblewrap, seccomp path filters) evaluates the resolved path, not the link. If that's how it resolves, every bot-repo mutation `vc-x1 push` attempts is denied before any network call happens. That would look nothing like a network failure in the error text, which is why I'd like to see the actual error from the sessions where this broke. Do you have it, or should I go dig it out of the transcripts? Right now we're reasoning from a hypothesis about a failure neither of us has the text for.

## The proposed command has a snag and a blind spot

`jj git push --named test-sandbox-push=@` will very likely fail before it touches the network. `@` is an empty commit with no description, and `jj git push` refuses to push commits with empty descriptions ("Won't push commit ... since it has no description"). That's still weakly informative, since a jj-level rejection tells us we got that far, but it doesn't test what we want to test.

The blind spot is bigger: a successful raw `jj git push` from the work repo exercises jj's https stack and the credential path, and nothing else. It says nothing about the bot repo, and nothing about `vc-x1 push`'s own code path, which after the jj-lib migration does its git work in-process through jj-lib rather than by spawning `jj`. In-process gix credential handling and subprocess jj credential handling are not guaranteed to behave the same.

## What I'd do instead

Cheap discriminators first, each one isolating a single layer, so a failure names its own cause:

1. `jj git remote list -R .claude` (is the bot repo still on ssh?)
2. `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://github.com` (raw https egress alive?)
3. `git ls-remote https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.git` (anonymous https read, no auth)
4. `git config --get-all credential.helper` and `gh auth status` (is there a credential helper at all? https push to GitHub needs a PAT, and if no helper is configured jj will try to prompt, which in a non-tty sandbox hangs or errors in a way that looks like a network problem but isn't)
5. a write probe into the bot repo, to settle the symlink question

Then the push test, using a commit that actually has a description. `jj git push --named test-sandbox-push=@-` points the bookmark at `main` (b90f948), which is already on the remote, so it creates a ref with zero objects to upload: it tests auth and ref-write cleanly. If you want to also test object upload, it needs a real throwaway described commit.

And cleanup matters: `jj bookmark delete test-sandbox-push` followed by a push of the deletion, or we leave a stray bookmark on GitHub.

One process note. This is a raw `jj git push`, which cuts against hard rule 1. I read that as a deliberate, named exception for diagnostics rather than drift, since the whole point is to test the layer underneath `vc-x1 push`. Flagging it so it's on the record rather than assumed. And when we get to actually running any of this, I'll ask for the push approval at the moment of pushing per rule 2.

**The plain version:** switching to https was almost certainly the right call, and ssh was almost certainly broken. But I suspect it wasn't the only thing broken, the bot repo probably still needs the same URL change, and I have a separate worry that I can't write to the bot repo at all under this sandbox. The one-command test you were given will probably fail for an unrelated reason (empty commit message) and wouldn't prove much even if it passed. I'd rather run four or five cheap checks that each isolate one layer, and I'd really like to see the original error text before we commit to a theory.

content.text:
"Read-only" was my own shorthand for "this command doesn't change anything," not a sandbox category. Nothing to do with the sandbox.

Concretely, `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '...' https://github.com` does an HTTP GET of GitHub's homepage, throws the response body away (`-o /dev/null`), and prints only the status code and elapsed time. Nothing is written to disk, nothing changes on GitHub, no credentials are involved. That's why I felt fine running it without waiting for your go-ahead, whereas changing a remote URL or pushing a bookmark I'd stop and ask for.

The sandbox is a separate axis. It constrains two things: which paths I can write to, and which hosts I can reach. `github.com` is on the network allowlist and `/dev/null` is on the write allowlist, so the sandbox would have permitted this command. It just wouldn't have permitted, say, `curl https://example.com`.

Where the sandbox actually bears on our investigation is the *push* path, not this probe. The reason I want this probe first is to establish a baseline: if plain https to github.com works, then any later failure in `git ls-remote` or `jj git push` is about credentials or jj's networking stack, not about basic egress. If it fails, we've learned the problem is far more fundamental than ssh-versus-https and everything downstream is moot.

Good, and thanks for the `.git` fix.

I like the reframe a lot better than my probe. Testing the real workflow end to end is the right call, because the thing we actually care about is whether `vc-x1 push` works, and a synthetic curl can pass while the real path still fails for reasons the probe never touched. My only concern is the mirror image of that: a real-workflow test has many ways to fail, and if it fails we need to know it failed *because of the sandbox* and not because of something incidental. So my thoughts are mostly about stripping out the other failure modes in advance.

## The proposed command will fail, but for a boring reason

`jj git push --named cc-bm-and-push-test=@` targets `@`, which right now is the empty, undescribed working-copy commit (twyksrvo). `jj git push` refuses to push commits with no description: "Won't push commit ... since it has no description." So we'd get a jj-level rejection before a single packet leaves the machine. That tells us nothing about the sandbox, and it's the kind of result that's easy to misread as "push is broken."

The syntax itself is right, incidentally. `--named NAME=REV` is the current way to create and push a new bookmark in one step, and it implies `--allow-new`. cw's shape is correct; it's only the revision that's wrong.

## Point it at `@-` instead

`@-` is `main` at b90f948, which is described and already on the remote. `jj git push --named cc-bm-and-push-test=@-` creates the remote ref with **zero objects to upload**, because GitHub already has that commit. That gives us a branch off main that's genuinely ready to develop on, which is exactly what you asked for, and it isolates one question cleanly: can I authenticate and write a ref over https? No object transfer, no cycle machinery, no bot repo. If that works, auth is proven. If it fails, we know it's auth or egress and nothing else.

Then the second half is the real test: `jj new` on the bookmark, create the test file, `vc-x1 push`. That exercises object upload, the dual-repo path, and vc-x1's own in-process jj-lib networking, all of which the first push deliberately leaves untested.

Splitting it this way costs one extra command and buys us an unambiguous read on any failure.

## Three confounds I'd clear first

**Credentials.** This is the one most likely to bite. Over ssh, auth was a key; over https, jj needs a git credential helper, and GitHub hasn't accepted passwords for years, so it needs a PAT or `gh auth git-credential`. If no helper is configured, jj will try to *prompt*, and in my non-interactive sandbox shell that either hangs until timeout or dies with something cryptic. It'd be easy to blame the sandbox for what is really a missing config. `git config --get-all credential.helper` is a config read that costs nothing and predicts the failure precisely. Worth noting your interactive shell and my sandboxed one may resolve helpers differently, so a helper that works for you at the terminal isn't automatically proof it works for me.

**The bot repo's bookmark.** We now have a bookmark in the work repo. What does `vc-x1 push` do on the bot side: create a matching bookmark, push to bot `main`, or fail because there's no counterpart? I don't know without reading the source, and it determines whether the second half of the experiment is even well-formed. Worth a look at `vc-x1 push --help` and the push code before we run it.

**vc-x1's own validation.** `vc-x1 push` is the cycle tool. It may well demand cycle scaffolding: a chores section, a TODO rung, a version bump, a title matching in three places per hard rule 9. A bare "add a test file" commit could be rejected by vc-x1's own rules, which would look like a failure but be entirely about protocol. Given `fix-todo` takes `--no-dry-run`, I'd bet vc-x1 has a dry-run convention; if `vc-x1 push` has one, that's an excellent instrument here, since it would exercise everything up to the network call and tell us what it wants before we commit to it.

## Two process notes

**Teardown.** This leaves a bookmark and a test file on GitHub in the work repo, plus whatever lands in the bot repo. I'd rather agree on the cleanup now than discover later we're not sure what's safe to delete: delete the bookmark locally, push the deletion, abandon the test commit. The bot-repo session commit is normal traffic, not litter, so that one stays.

**Hard rule 3.** The `vc-x1 push` is a push, so the turn ends there: closing words before the invoke, then nothing from me until you speak. That means verifying on GitHub can't happen in the same turn as the push. Fine, just worth planning for so it doesn't look like I stalled. And per rule 2 I'll ask for approval at the moment of each push rather than treating this discussion as blanket authorization.

I'd also gently note the bookmark name. Your convention in this repo is `<topic>-vc-x1` (`trapezoid-push-vc-x1`, `drop-sync-state-vc-x1`). `cc-bm-and-push-test` breaks that pattern. For a throwaway that's arguably fine and even useful as a visual marker that it's not a real cycle, but if you'd rather keep the convention uniform it's `sandbox-push-test-vc-x1` or similar. Your call.

**The plain version:** your plan is better than mine, but the exact command fails because `@` is an empty commit with no message. Point it at `@-` instead and it works with nothing to upload, which cleanly proves auth. Before the `vc-x1 push` half, I want to check three things that could make it fail for reasons having nothing to do with the sandbox: whether a credential helper exists, what vc-x1 does about the bot repo's bookmark, and whether vc-x1 will even accept a commit that isn't a real cycle rung.

Two caveats. Whether the stored token is still valid and still carries `repo` scope, we can't know without using it. And note the asymmetry: reading `~/.gitcreds` is permitted, but *writing* it is not, since it's outside my write allowlist. So if the credential were ever missing or in need of refresh, the store helper's write-back would fail. The read path is what we need, and that's fine.

## vc-x1 push --help killed two of my three confounds

**The bot bookmark worry was unfounded.** "The bot repo always advances `main`." There is no bot-side bookmark to create. That question is closed.

**The validation worry was unfounded too.** "vc-x1 runs no build or test steps: run your project's checks yourself before pushing." It's a mechanical commit-and-push tool with two approval gates, not a cycle-protocol enforcer. It won't reject our test file for lacking a chores section or a version bump.

**And `--dry-run` exists**, described as "print the exact commands for every stage without side effects." That's precisely the instrument I hoped for.

## But it surfaced a new top suspect, and it isn't the sandbox

> Non-interactive use: pass both `--title` and `--body` plus `--yes` to skip both gates.

`vc-x1 push` has two interactive gates: a diff review, and a message stage that opens `$EDITOR`. My shell is non-interactive with no tty. If a past session ran `vc-x1 push` without all three of `--title`, `--body`, and `--yes`, the message stage would try to spawn an editor and either hang until something killed it or die with an error that looks nothing like its actual cause. That would reproduce "vc-x1 push fails at the end of a session" perfectly, and it has nothing whatsoever to do with ssh, https, or the sandbox.

I'd rate this at least as likely as the network theory for the historical failures. It's also trivially falsifiable: we're going to pass all three flags this time regardless, so if the push now succeeds we won't have distinguished the two causes. Worth deciding whether you want to know which one it was, because that's a different experiment (reproduce the old failure deliberately) than the one we're running.

## And a second, sharper suspect

`vc-x1` is mid-migration to doing its git work **in-process through jj-lib** rather than by spawning `jj`. Credential-helper support in jj has historically lived in the CLI layer, not in jj-lib: jj-lib's push takes a credentials callback, and the CLI is what implements "shell out to `git credential fill`." If vc-x1 calls jj-lib directly without reimplementing that, then over https it has no way to reach `~/.gitcreds`, and we'd see a very specific signature: **`jj git push` succeeds and `vc-x1 push` fails on authentication.** Under ssh this may have been invisible, because libgit2 can pick up an agent or a default key path without any helper.

This is exactly why splitting the experiment into a raw `jj git push` followed by a `vc-x1 push` matters. The two halves test different credential stacks, and a difference between them is diagnostic rather than confusing.

One more small thing from the help: `--allow-jj-mismatch` implies vc-x1 aborts when the installed `jj -V` disagrees with its linked jj-lib. Another way a run dies for reasons unrelated to the network, and worth knowing before we blame the sandbox.

Still untested: whether I can write into the bot repo through the `.claude` symlink. `--dry-run` won't tell us, since it has no side effects. The `commit-bot` stage is where that would surface.

**The plain version:** credentials look fine and I can read them. The help file cleared up two of my worries and handed us a dry-run mode. But it raised a better suspect than the sandbox: `vc-x1 push` wants an interactive editor unless you pass `--title`, `--body`, and `--yes`, which would hang a session like mine. And there's a real chance vc-x1's in-process jj-lib path can't reach the credential store at all, which we'd spot as `jj git push` working while `vc-x1 push` fails.

My suggested next step is a quick grep through vc-x1's source for how it supplies credentials to jj-lib, since if that comes back empty we can predict the failure before running it. Then `vc-x1 push --dry-run`. Say the word.

content.text:
Found it, and it kills my credential hypothesis in a way that strengthens yours.

## vc-x1's push is literally `git push` in a subprocess

`src/jj/session.rs:612-621`:

```rust
let git_settings = GitSettings::from_settings(&self.settings)?;
let stats = git::push_refs(
    tx.repo_mut(),
    git_settings.to_subprocess_options(),
    remote,
    &ref_updates,
    &mut DebugCallback,
    &GitPushOptions::default(),
)?;
```

That `to_subprocess_options()` is the whole answer. jj-lib 0.43 performs remote operations by **spawning the real `git` binary** rather than doing the network work in-process through libgit2 or gix. `grep -i credential` over `src/` returns nothing precisely because vc-x1 never needs to handle credentials: it delegates to `git`, which reads `credential.helper` from your config, which reads `~/.gitcreds`.

So the concern I raised last turn, that the in-process jj-lib path might not reach the credential store, is wrong. There is no in-process network path. `vc-x1 push`, `jj git push`, and plain `git push` all converge on the same `git` process with the same config, the same credential helper, and the same transport. The `DebugCallback` passed alongside is a progress/sideband sink, not a credentials callback.

## Which makes the ssh story fully coherent for the first time

Before your URL change, that spawned `git` would have been handed `git@github.com:...`, so it would invoke ssh. In my sandbox, ssh fails twice over: the read policy denies `~/.ssh` except the commit-signing key and `known_hosts`, so there's no auth key to offer, and a host-allowlist proxy can't recognize a port-22 connection to github.com, so the egress is blocked too. The spawned `git` inherits every one of my sandbox restrictions, since it's an ordinary child process.

That is a complete, mechanism-level explanation of the end-of-session push failures, and it predicts that your switch to https fixes them: `git` now speaks TLS to an allowlisted host and pulls a token from a file I'm allowed to read.

It also explains why this never bit you at your own terminal. Same tool, same code path, no sandbox.

## What's still unproven

**Egress.** I still haven't confirmed https to github.com actually leaves this box, since you stopped the curl. It's presumably fine, but it's an assumption, and the first real push will test it either way.

**Bot repo writes.** This is now the only hypothesis I have left that could still bite. The `commit-bot` and `squash-push-bot` stages write into `.claude`, which resolves through the symlink to `~/.claude/projects/...`. My write allowlist covers the project directory and a handful of others but does not include `~/.claude/projects`, and the deny list names it explicitly. Linux sandboxing evaluates the resolved path, not the link, so this could fail. I can read there fine, as `jj git remote list -R .claude` proved, but reads were never in question.

`--dry-run` won't settle it, since it has no side effects by design. The cheap way to settle it is a one-line probe: create a file under `.claude/tmp/` and delete it. If the create is denied, we know before we ever start a push, and we know the failure is filesystem rather than network. That's a write into your bot repo, trivially reversible, but I'll hold since you're pacing this.

One footnote worth filing: because the network leg is a `git` subprocess, `vc-x1 push` will also inherit any git proxy config and any `insteadOf` rewrite rules. Nothing suggests you have those, but if a stale `url.git@github.com:.insteadOf` rule existed anywhere in your config it would silently undo the https switch. A quick `git config --get-regexp 'url\..*\.insteadof'` would rule it out.

**The plain version:** vc-x1 doesn't do its own networking at all. It shells out to `git`, so it uses your normal credential helper, and your https switch should fix it. The ssh theory now has a complete mechanism behind it: the spawned `git` inherits my sandbox, which blocks both the ssh key and port 22. The one thing that could still go wrong is writing to the bot repo through the `.claude` symlink, which a two-second probe would settle.

content.text:
The write probe **passed**, and the reason is more interesting than I expected. Two findings:

## The bot repo is not where AGENTS.md says it is

`readlink -f .claude` returns `/home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/.claude`. It is a **real directory inside the project root**, not a symlink pointing out to `~/.claude/projects/`. The link runs the *other* direction: `~/.claude/projects/-home-wink-data-prgs-rust-vc-x1` is the symlink, and it points back into the project. My earlier `ls` missed the probe file only because I tacked an extra `/.claude` onto the path; the projects entry *is* the bot repo, not a parent of it.

That settles hypothesis 2 completely. The bot repo's real path sits inside `/home/wink/data/prgs/rust`, squarely within my write allowlist, so `commit-bot` and `squash-push-bot` can write. Proven empirically, not inferred: touch succeeded, the file appeared in both listings, rm succeeded, and the probe is cleaned up.

Worth noting AGENTS.md describes this as "symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`", with a trailing `/.claude` that doesn't exist and a direction that reads backwards. That's a pinned template file, so per hard rule 12 I won't touch it, but it looks like `notes/dogfood.md` material.

## But the listing exposed something that may matter much more

Look at these entries in the bot repo:

```
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 agents
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 commands
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 hooks
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 launch.json
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 loop.md
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 output-styles
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 routines
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 scheduled_tasks.json
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 settings.json
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 skills
crw-rw-rw- 1 nobody nobody 1, 3 Aug  7 08:44 workflows
```

Character device, major 1 minor 3, owned by nobody. That is `/dev/null` **bind-mounted over each path**. This is how my sandbox enforces its denylist: rather than failing the syscall, it replaces those paths with /dev/null so reads return empty and writes vanish. All eleven are on the deny list I was shown, and all eleven live inside the bot repo.

The concern: the bot repo is a jj/git working copy, and `vc-x1 push`'s `commit-bot` stage snapshots it. If any of those paths are **tracked**, jj's snapshot sees a tracked regular file or directory replaced by a character device. Depending on how jj handles an unsupported file type, that's either a hard error during snapshot or, worse, a silent recording of those files as deleted, producing a bot commit that removes `settings.json`, `hooks/`, `skills/`, and the rest.

That would be a failure at `commit-bot`, before any network call, in a session run under a sandbox and not when you run vc-x1 yourself. It fits the symptom at least as well as the ssh theory does, and unlike the ssh theory it is not fixed by your URL change.

I want to check whether those paths are actually tracked before saying more, since if they're all gitignored this is a non-issue. The safe way is `git -C .claude ls-files`, which reads the index without triggering a jj snapshot. I'm deliberately reaching for git over jj here despite hard rule 6, precisely because `jj status` would snapshot the working copy and that's the operation I'm trying not to perform blind. Say go and I'll run that plus a look at the bot repo's `.gitignore`.

**The plain version:** I can write to the bot repo fine, so that worry is dead, and AGENTS.md has the symlink description backwards. But the listing revealed that my sandbox masks eleven paths inside the bot repo by mounting /dev/null over them, and if the bot repo tracks any of those files, the `commit-bot` stage could error or commit spurious deletions. That's a new suspect the https switch does nothing about, and I'd like to check it before we push anything.

Snapshot succeeded cleanly. jj silently skipped all eleven character devices rather than erroring or trying to auto-track them, and the only working-copy changes are the two you'd expect: this session's transcript being added, and `settings.local.json` modified. Hypothesis 3 is dead.

## Where the investigation stands

Every alternative explanation I raised has now been eliminated empirically rather than argued away:

- **Credentials**: fine. vc-x1 doesn't do its own networking; `git_settings.to_subprocess_options()` means jj-lib spawns the real `git` binary, which reads `credential.helper = store --file ~/.gitcreds`, and that file exists with a github.com entry I'm allowed to read.
- **Bot repo writes**: fine. It's a real directory inside the project root, well within my write allowlist. Probe wrote and deleted successfully.
- **Masked paths**: fine. Untracked, so nothing can be recorded as deleted, and jj's snapshot skips character devices without complaint.
- **`$EDITOR` hang**: you confirmed `--yes --title --body` works.

What's left is exactly the original hypothesis, and it now has a complete mechanism behind it. `vc-x1 push` spawns `git`; that child inherits my sandbox; under the old ssh URL it had no readable key (`~/.ssh` is denied except the signing key) and no route on port 22 (a host-allowlist proxy can't identify an ssh connection). Your switch to https should fix both, because `git` now speaks TLS to an allowlisted host and reads a token from a file I can open.

The one thing still untested is whether that actually works, which is the experiment.

## Proposed run

**Step A**, the bookmark, pointed at `@-` rather than `@`:

```
jj git push --named cc-bm-and-push-test=@-
```

`@-` is `main` at b90f948, which is described and already on GitHub, so this uploads zero objects and does nothing but create a remote ref. That isolates one question: can I authenticate and write a ref over https? Pointing at `@` would fail on jj's no-description check and tell us nothing. This gives you the branch-ready-to-develop-on you asked for, branched off main.

**Step B**, next turn: create a test file, then

```
vc-x1 push cc-bm-and-push-test --title ... --body ... --yes
```

which exercises object upload, `commit-bot`, and `squash-push-bot`'s force-update of bot `main`. Splitting it means a failure in B after a success in A points squarely at vc-x1's path rather than at auth.

**Teardown**, once we've verified on GitHub: delete the bookmark locally and push the deletion, abandon the test commit. The bot-repo commit stays, since session records are normal traffic rather than litter.

Two things to note before you decide. Step A is a push, so per hard rule 2 I'm asking for its approval now rather than treating this discussion as authorization. And per hard rule 3 my turn ends at the push, so verifying on GitHub happens after you speak again.

**The plain version:** every competing theory is now ruled out by an actual test, and the ssh explanation is the only one standing. I'm ready to run `jj git push --named cc-bm-and-push-test=@-`, which creates the branch on GitHub with nothing to upload and proves whether https auth works. Approve and I'll run it.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## File reads: read the slice you need
12	
13	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
14	further on demand.
15	
16	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
17	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
18	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read further only when chasing a
19	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
20	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
21	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it first.
22	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
23	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
24	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
25	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
26	  need.
27	
28	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
29	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
30	to historical files.
31	
32	## Notes references
33	
34	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
35	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
36	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
37	single-bracketed.
38	
39	## Reference numbering
40	
41	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
42	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
43	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
44	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
45	
46	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
47	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
48	file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
49	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
50	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
51	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
52	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
53	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
54	
55	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
56	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
57	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
58	as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
59	exact shape.
60	
61	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
62	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
63	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
64	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
65	definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
66	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
67	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
68	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
69	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
70	slots out of document order).
71	
72	## Markdown anchor links
73	
74	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
75	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
76	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
77	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
78	official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
79	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
80	
81	## Todo format
82	
83	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
84	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
85	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
86	description with reference links to more detail.
87	
88	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
89	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
90	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
91	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
92	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
93	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
94	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
95	
96	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
97	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
98	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
99	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
100	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
101	
102	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
103	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
104	
105	Example shape:
106	
107	```
108	# Todo
109	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
110	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
111	
112	# Done
113	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
114	
115	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
116	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
117	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
118	```
119	
120	## Retiring Done entries
121	
122	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
123	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
124	
125	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
126	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
127	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
128	  version-of-record.
129	
130	Migration mechanics:
131	
132	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
133	  number).
134	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
135	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
136	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
137	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
138	
139	## Chores conventions
140	
141	### Headings and entries that record a commit
142	
143	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
144	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
145	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
146	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
147	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
148	[Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
149	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
150	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
151	title.
152	
153	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
154	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
155	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
156	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
157	
158	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
159	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
160	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
161	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
162	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
163	
164	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
165	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
166	
167	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
168	
169	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
170	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
171	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
172	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
173	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
180	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
181	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
182	
183	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
184	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
185	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
186	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
187	direction).
188	
189	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
190	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
191	narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
192	
193	### Chores commit references
194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader
202	
203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
204	- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader
205	
206	<intro paragraph...>
207	```
208	
209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
213	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
215	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
216	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
218	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
219	
220	```
221	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
222	```
223	
224	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
234	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
253

before editing a notes file.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## File reads: read the slice you need

further on demand.

- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
  need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
to historical files.

## Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's

- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).

ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only

cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
the pointer, so the two don't drift.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

This overrides versioning.md "Dev artifact name" in mechanism, not intent; dogfooded here
first, the template proposal follows.

### Why the file is unsound and the op log is not

The state file answers "where was the repo before the sync" and is blind to everything after
its write. `revert` ran `jj op restore` to it with no guard, so one commit after a failed
sync, "undo the sync" and "rewind to the snapshot" silently diverge and revert discards the
difference. No file-side fix closes that: presence-as-semaphore says nothing about intervening
operations.

jj's op log holds the same answer without the blindness: identify sync's operations, derive the
revert target as the parent of the most recent sync run's earliest op, and, decisively, detect
and refuse intervening non-sync operations. One honest prerequisite: only sync's fetch runs
through the in-process session today; its reposition and rebase steps still spawn the installed
jj (`jj new` / `jj rebase`, as do `op log` / `op restore` themselves), whose ops carry jj's
stock descriptions, so "identifiable sync operations" first means migrating those spawns, a
remainder 0.78.0's "ending jj and git subprocess spawning" claim reads as having finished but
did not (found 2026-08-06 at this cycle's review; tracked in the `## Todo` entry "Retire the
remaining jj spawns; make the build enforce it"). That derived-not-persisted design is the
bar any `revert` reintroduction must clear; until someone wants it, `jj op log` +
`jj op restore` is the documented recovery, shown by sync's failure report and README.

# References

[1]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/a8b43a18999e "a8b43a18999ece30e7b807650ba45eb9b236ebdc"
[2]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/b2a5171292c5 "b2a5171292c553d000d6ead88fc5f5e537bebb7c"

## test: sandbox push probe

- [[N]] test: sandbox push probe

`vc-x1 push` had been failing from sandboxed sessions, and the cause was never pinned down: the
failure always arrived at the end of a session, where the cheapest response was to hand the push
to wink and move on. This commit is the controlled experiment, run one step at a time so each
layer could be cleared separately. The rung carries no version because this is not a cycle rung:
it publishes a disposable marker on its own `cc-bm-and-push-test` bookmark, is not merged to
main, and the bookmark becomes a tag so the record persists.

The cause, confirmed: both repos were originally cloned over ssh, and the sandbox denies ssh
twice over. Reads of `~/.ssh` are blocked except the commit-signing key and `known_hosts`, so no
auth key is available, and we think a host allowlist cannot admit a port-22 connection at all,
since ssh carries no SNI or Host header for a filter to match on. wink repointed both remotes at
https before the experiment, which is what made the push work.

- the network leg is a spawned `git`: `git_push_bookmark` hands
  `git_settings.to_subprocess_options()` to `jj_lib::git::push_refs`, so jj-lib runs the real
  `git` binary instead of doing the transfer in-process. That child inherits the sandbox, which
  is why a sandboxed run and wink's own terminal diverge on identical config
- credentials follow from that: git's own `store --file ~/.gitcreds` helper serves both repos,
  the sandbox permits reading it, and vc-x1 needs no credential callback of its own
- three competing hypotheses were killed by test rather than by argument. The bot repo is a real
  directory inside the project root, so it sits inside the write allowlist. The config paths the
  sandbox masks inside `.claude` are untracked, so no snapshot can record them as deleted. And
  jj's snapshot skips the character devices those masked paths become, without erroring
- the interactive-editor hypothesis died separately: `vc-x1 push` opens `$EDITOR` unless
  `--title`, `--body`, and `--yes` are all supplied, which would hang a non-interactive session,
  but wink confirmed the three-flag form works

One finding for the dogfood log: AGENTS.md places the bot repo at a symlink from
`~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`, which has one path component too many and
the direction reversed. `<project>/.claude` is the real directory, and the `projects` entry is
the symlink pointing in.

# References

[1]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/a8b43a18999e "a8b43a18999ece30e7b807650ba45eb9b236ebdc"

1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running
4	artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
5	unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
6	this file is copied **verbatim**, with
7	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
8	covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
9	edits.
10	
11	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit
12	here. Project overrides go in [custom.md](../custom.md).
13	
14	## Terms
15	
16	Three names, used as defined here across
17	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
18	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
19	
20	- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
21	  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
22	  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
23	  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
24	- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
25	  version, in the project's manifest (see
26	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
27	  a built or running artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## Grammar and storage
31	
32	One prose spelling everywhere (ladders, chores, commit
33	bullets, conversation):
34	
35	```
36	<public>[-<suffix>]
37	```
38	
39	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
40	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters
41	  or digits; usually integers (`3`, `3.1`, `3.1.0`), an
42	  alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed, sparingly.
43	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that
44	  opens the suffix: never a dash inside the suffix, never a
45	  `+` in the prose form. This is the portability invariant
46	  that makes the version storable in every medium below.
47	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**:
48	  commit bullets and prose may write `v0.78.0-3.1` for
49	  scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440
50	  ignores a leading `v`; Cargo rejects one.)
51	
52	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
53	
54	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim; the
55	  suffix rides in the prerelease slot, valid at any dot
56	  depth.
57	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`:
58	  `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`. Mechanical and bijective
59	  because there is exactly one dash to find.
60	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one
61	  `-`; else the `+` remap; a new medium adds its case to
62	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
63	
64	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
65	
66	- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.**
67	  SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before* its bare release
68	  (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out);
69	  PEP 440 sorts the remapped form *after* it, and
70	  reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite
71	  directions, so no cross-medium logic may compare stored
72	  versions; ordering truth lives in the ladder and git
73	  history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a
74	  version gate) is unaffected.
75	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer
76	  build-metadata use in Rust repos even though Cargo allows
77	  it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with
78	  the Python spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares
79	  the deviation in its `custom.md`.
80	
81	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a
82	sibling repo rejected every multi-dash version outright, and
83	the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
84	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`,
85	`1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second `+` are all
86	invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any
87	depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but silently becomes the
88	post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is
89	the largest form every medium accepts.
90	
91	## Recording the version-of-record
92	
93	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
94	surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
95	your medium:
96	
97	- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
98	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
99	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
100	    committed config it's sourced from)
101	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
102	    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
103	    needed
104	- **Notation**: how the `-` form is stored; see
105	  [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
106	  - verbatim where the format allows the one `-` (TOML
107	    `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`)
108	  - the `+` remap where it bars it (PEP 440, e.g. a Python
109	    project): `0.3.0-5.3.0` -> `0.3.0+5.3.0`, same version,
110	    just the stored spelling
111	- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
112	  version-of-record:
113	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
114	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
115	- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
116	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
117	  this project follows the per-commit preference.
118	
119	## Dev artifact name
120	
121	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the
122	installed CLI) while this repo is under active development,
123	the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle
124	install never clobbers the binary consumers are running:
125	
126	- **Name** — the manifest's package name carries a `-dev`
127	  suffix (`vc-x1` → `vc-x1-dev`); if Rust, `[package].name`,
128	  so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces
129	  `<name>-dev` and leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
130	- **Constant, not per-step** — the step already lives in the
131	  version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V` reports the exact rung);
132	  a per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and
133	  litter the install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion** — plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit
135	  act: a separate clone built at the chosen commit with the
136	  plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the
137	  per-commit flow's install.
138	
139	This project adopted the convention 2026-07-23 (during
140	0.75.0); projects without external consumers can skip it.
141	
142	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
143	
144	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
145	on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
146	the exact commit it came from.
147	
148	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
149	  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
150	  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
151	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
152	  if it differs.
153	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are
154	  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
155	  contain (see the cycle protocol's
156	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
157	
158	## Step numbering
159	
160	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see
161	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes each commit's
162	phase in the version suffix — the **final identifier `0` marks
163	a Preparation**:
164	
165	- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation
166	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits
167	- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
168	
169	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
170	no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
171	Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
172	needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
173	grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
174	renumbering siblings.
175	
176	Disambiguation:
177	
178	- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
179	  Preparation.
180	- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
181	  identifier `0`).
182	
183	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
184	
185	- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
186	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
187	- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
188	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
189	
190	Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
191	active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
192	every commit carries a distinct version.

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:

covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit
here. Project overrides go in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),

  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
  a built or running artifact derives from it.
- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.

## Grammar and storage

One prose spelling everywhere (ladders, chores, commit
bullets, conversation):

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters
  or digits; usually integers (`3`, `3.1`, `3.1.0`), an
  alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed, sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that
  opens the suffix: never a dash inside the suffix, never a
  `+` in the prose form. This is the portability invariant
  that makes the version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**:
  commit bullets and prose may write `v0.78.0-3.1` for
  scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440
  ignores a leading `v`; Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim; the
  suffix rides in the prerelease slot, valid at any dot
  depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`:
  `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`. Mechanical and bijective
  because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one
  `-`; else the `+` remap; a new medium adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.**
  SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before* its bare release
  (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out);
  PEP 440 sorts the remapped form *after* it, and
  reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite
  directions, so no cross-medium logic may compare stored
  versions; ordering truth lives in the ladder and git
  history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a
  version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer
  build-metadata use in Rust repos even though Cargo allows
  it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with
  the Python spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares
  the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a
sibling repo rejected every multi-dash version outright, and
the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`,
`1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second `+` are all
invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any
depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but silently becomes the
post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is
the largest form every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation**: how the `-` form is stored; see
  [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - verbatim where the format allows the one `-` (TOML
    `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`)
  - the `+` remap where it bars it (PEP 440, e.g. a Python
    project): `0.3.0-5.3.0` -> `0.3.0+5.3.0`, same version,
    just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the
installed CLI) while this repo is under active development,
the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle
install never clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name** — the manifest's package name carries a `-dev`
  suffix (`vc-x1` → `vc-x1-dev`); if Rust, `[package].name`,
  so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces
  `<name>-dev` and leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step** — the step already lives in the
  version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V` reports the exact rung);
  a per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and
  litter the install dir with stale binaries.

  act: a separate clone built at the chosen commit with the
  plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the
  per-commit flow's install.
